key_clinical_evidence: The critical DWI discriminator: pyogenic abscess causes CENTRAL restricted diffusion within the pus cavity (the central ADC is low); high-grade glioma causes PERIPHERAL restricted diffusion at the hypercellular enhancing rim (the central necrotic core has facilitated diffusion). This case shows peripheral rim restriction without central restriction — a pattern inconsistent with abscess.

MR perfusion (rCBV) is the most powerful non-invasive discriminator: abscess rCBV is low (<1.0) because the rim is reactive inflammatory tissue without tumor angiogenesis; high-grade glioma rCBV is markedly elevated (>1.75, often 2.5-4.0) due to pathological neovascularization. rCBV 3.1 in this case excludes abscess.

MR spectroscopy provides additional discrimination: abscess produces amino acid peaks (acetate at 1.92 ppm, succinate at 2.4 ppm, alanine at 1.47 ppm) from bacterial fermentation; high-grade glioma produces elevated Cho/NAA without these peaks. Absence of amino acid peaks in this case further argues against abscess.

The low-grade fever (37.9°C), mildly elevated CRP/ESR, and recent dental procedure are classic red herrings that anchor toward abscess; however, procalcitonin is normal, blood cultures are negative, and the dental source was minor (crown replacement, not abscess drainage with uncontrolled infection) — the infective source is insufficient to explain a 3.4 cm intracranial lesion.

Irregular nodular rim enhancement is a morphological feature favoring neoplasm; abscess typically produces a thin, smooth, medially thin-walled ring (the medial wall is thinner due to differential blood supply). This case shows a thick, irregular, nodular rim — inconsistent with the expected abscess morphology.
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue — stereotactic biopsy with dual submission to pathology and microbiology ensures that abscess is microbiologically excluded even if imaging strongly favors tumor.

results.authors: Law M, Yang S, Wang H, et al.
results.key_finding: Relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) >1.75 in the enhancing lesion has high sensitivity and specificity for high-grade glioma versus low-grade glioma. Brain abscesses demonstrate low rCBV (<1.0 in most series) because the enhancing rim reflects reactive inflammatory tissue without neovascularization, in contrast to the angiogenic vasculature of high-grade gliomas.
results.title: Glioma grading: sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values of perfusion MR imaging and proton MR spectroscopy

results.authors: Bulik M, Jancalek R, Vanicek J, et al.
results.key_finding: Markedly elevated choline (Cho/NAA ratio >2.0, Cho/Cr ratio >2.5) with reduced NAA is characteristic of high-grade glioma. Pyogenic abscess shows absent or markedly reduced choline and NAA, with presence of amino acid peaks (succinate, acetate, alanine) at 1.3–1.9 ppm on short-echo MRS, which are absent in tumor.

Definitive diagnosis requires tissue. Imaging alone cannot distinguish GBM from abscess or metastasis with certainty.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge_notes: This is the first GBM-vs-abscess ring-enhancement diagnostic puzzle in the GLIO-HG set. The case tests whether the agent correctly interprets the DWI pattern (peripheral vs. central restriction), orders and integrates MR perfusion (high rCBV excludes abscess) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho without amino acid peaks excludes abscess), and resists premature closure on the abscess diagnosis despite three embedded red herrings (low-grade fever, recent dental procedure with peri-apical inflammation, and mildly elevated CRP/ESR). The emergency physician's impression of 'abscess more likely' is a deliberate anchoring cue that a competent agent must override via systematic imaging interpretation.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools (MRI, labs, literature search, neurosurgery consult, neuro-oncology consult), 2 recommended tools (perfusion MRI, MR spectroscopy), 3 embedded red herrings (fever, dental history, inflammatory markers); requires cross-modal synthesis of DWI pattern + rCBV + MRS amino acid absence to exclude abscess; ER physician anchoring cue adds cognitive anchoring pressure

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 55-year-old right-handed South Asian male, a mathematics teacher, who presents with a 3-week history of progressive right-sided pulsatile headache, left arm weakness, and mild difficulty with calculations and word retrieval. He initially attributed the headache to stress and fatigue following a dental crown replacement procedure performed on his lower right first molar 3 weeks ago under local anesthesia. At that visit, the dentist noted mild peri-apical inflammation on pre-procedure radiograph, which was treated with the crown; the patient completed a 5-day prophylactic course of amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily post-procedure (completed approximately 2 weeks ago). His wife first noticed left arm clumsiness about 2 weeks ago when he kept dropping objects, and more recently he has had episodes of forgetting students' names and making arithmetic errors on the blackboard, which is completely out of character. He describes the headache as progressively worsening, worse in the morning and when bending forward, different in quality from any previous headaches, and not fully relieved by acetaminophen. He has had no seizures, no loss of consciousness, no fever at home (family noted 'he felt warm' on one occasion last week), no nausea or vomiting, no neck stiffness, and no rash. He denies weight loss, night sweats, or known exposure to sick contacts. On arrival to the emergency department, a non-contrast CT head was performed and revealed a ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal-parietal region with surrounding edema and mild mass effect, prompting urgent neurology admission and MRI. Given the recent dental procedure with documented peri-apical inflammation, the emergency physician charted an impression of 'ring-enhancing lesion — brain abscess vs. neoplasm, abscess more likely given dental source.'
